I break infosec into three BROAD categories: development, networking and systems. Development is concerned with writing code. Networking deals with things like firewalls, routers, switches, IDS/IPS, and similar systems. Systems is concerned with application platforms, operating systems, and the like.

I maintain that you have to be a master of ONE of those fields and at least modestly capable in the other two if you want to be successful in infosec.

That's my take.

If you're looking for specific references, or sites that would be relevant, I suggest the defcon forums (at forum.defcon.org), hackforums.net and antionline.com. If you want to get a flavor for the community, you should give consideration to attending Black Hat US AND DEFCON -- they give two different feels for the community. If there's a B-Sides near you, attend. If you're close KY, go to DerbyCON.

Hello Bazman.

I have a bit of experience in this area and I believe I could provide you with some advice, but first, I would like to know more about what you actually wish to accomplish. The concept of "hacking" is very broad and can mean different things to different people. With a better idea of what you would like to learn how to do, I can suggest some appropriate subjects for you to study on this path.

I would first clarify that "hacking" and "pen testing" are very different trades that would involve different types of paths for you to follow.

A hacker might disassemble or reverse engineer a program or service, discover vulnerabilities in the programs' coding, and develop exploit code to leverage the vulnerability to do something interesting or useful. The result is a shiny new hack spawned from the creativity and unconventional engineering skills of the hacker.

A pen tester might use automated tools to subject a target system to dozens or hundreds of pre-existing exploits to test the target for known vulnerabilities, possibly resulting in a penetration of the system. The pen tester need not know how to discover the vulnerabilities in the first place, or how to develop them in to an exploit. The pen tester doesn't even necessarily need to know how to program. The pen tester needs only know how to use the testing software to scan machines and understand the results. An example of pen testing software would be something like Metasploit, or any of the professional alternatives.

So to put it simply, pen testing will make sure a machine is up to date and not vulnerable to exploits that hackers have already discovered.

Hacking is discovering vulnerabilities and creating exploits where none existed previously.

In my opinion, being a hacker is a lifelong quest to expand your technical knowledge and a creative itch to do interesting things, while being a pen tester is about utilizing the knowledge of the hackers for the practical purpose of securing systems.

Get yourself a good book on TCP/IP.

Get a decent understanding of a compiled language like C, and memory management.

Then learn a decent high level language, like Python for automating stuff.

There are tons of tools ad PoCs out there that can be used to acquire shells all day long, but if you don't know how they work down in the nitty gritty, you'll be just another skid.

Acquire knowledge, and apply it.
